data.raw_text:
The Mole People (3)

When people lose their home - life can sometimes be a bitch - and they are desperate and have no place to go to, they might follow a very old instinct. Look for a cave to hide in, the deeper, the better. Survival.

People (this can happen to everybody!) are typically driven by poverty, addiction, mental health issues, displacement, and extreme weather, with people using forgotten infrastructure (storm drains, sewers, quarries, caves, abandoned subways) for shelter. Raids, floods, disease, and violence are common risks.

In the previous two posts I wrote about the mole people in New York City and Bucharest (Romania). But these are not the only cities where people chose to hide underground.

Las Vegas, USA (Storm Drain Tunnels)

Las Vegas has roughly 600 miles (!) of flood-control storm tunnels built in the 1990s. Estimates from 2024 - 2026) put 1,200 – 1,500 people living in them, more during spikes in homelessness. They seek refuge from scorching heat (over 120°F/49°C) above ground in summer, and freezing nights in winter. 

Many create “homes” with beds, furniture, TVs, even showers, often near the Strip’s casinos. Dangers include flash floods (which can sweep people away), rats, disease, and extreme temperatures inside (up to 50°C reported in some accounts). 

Raids and construction projects periodically clear sections, but the population persists amid Las Vegas’s broader homelessness crisis (over 7,000–8,000 counted in recent point-in-time surveys).

Paris, France (Catacombs and Quarries)

Paris sits atop hundreds of miles (over 200–300 km) of abandoned limestone quarries and tunnels, part of which became the famous Catacombs (ossuaries with millions of bones). 

The official tourist section is monitored, but the vast “off-limits” network (illegal to enter) attracts cataphiles (urban explorers) and, at times, homeless individuals or small groups.

Signs of habitation (makeshift camps, graffiti, warnings like “do not try to find us”) have been reported, though not on the scale of NYC or Vegas. The tunnels offer hiding spots but are dangerous - collapses, flooding, disorientation. 

Historically used in wars and by the Resistance; today, they’re more a fringe squatter/party scene than stable communities. Enforcement and barriers limit long-term stays. There are secret (pop-up) restaurants, bars, and even a cinema.

Manila, Philippines: Flood-control tunnels under busy highways house communities of families (one report mentioned over 100 families in a single tunnel section). Designed for water but used for shelter in a dense, flood-prone city.

Los Angeles, USA: Storm drains and canals in South LA and other areas see homeless encampments, especially in flood channels. Similar risks of flooding and poor sanitation.

Other U.S. cities: Chicago, Boston, and others have had reports of people in utility tunnels or abandoned infrastructure, though usually smaller and less documented than NYC/Las Vegas.

Historical/ancient parallels: 
Derinkuyu and other Cappadocia underground cities in Turkey are very old; once housed thousands, now tourist sites.
Coober Pedy, Australia is a modern opal-mining town with many underground homes dug for heat relief, but legal and above-ground-adjacent living. 
These are intentional subterranean settlements, not desperation-driven.

If you like to read the earlier posts about the Mole People you can find them on my profile under 'Highlights'.

Pic: The Paris catacombs and cemeteries
